**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 18, 2026
**Re:** Peitort / Elmcrest: Buyer-side review of transaction documents (Stock Purchase Agreement dated September 14, 2026)
**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## I. Executive Summary

I reviewed all nine documents in the folder:

- the Stock Purchase Agreement (SPA);
- the Disclosure Schedule;
- Peitort's board consent;
- the Sallow Key Employee Agreement;
- Seller's draft side letter;
- the form of Seller Note (Exhibit B);
- the June 2026 LOI;
- the closing-logistics email thread; and
- the Mutual Confidentiality Agreement (MCA).

The SPA is signed. Closing is targeted for the week of December 7, 2026, and the California Board of Pharmacy approval is the only Required Consent still outstanding.

I found six substantive issues adverse to Peitort, plus some minor points. Three need attention before Closing. Our leverage drops sharply once we close and once the Seller Note is executed.

**URGENT: action needed before Closing**

1. **Orlund change-of-control consent (Issue 6).**
   - Peitort must close even if Orlund has not consented.
   - If Orlund then terminates the Velnarix license, Peitort has no recourse.
   - The email thread shows nobody is tracking this consent.
2. **Seller side letter, Section 2 (Issue 2).**
   - Section 2 removes the regulatory-compliance carve-out from the $18,600,000 General Cap.
   - **Do not sign it in its current form.**
3. **Seller Note execution version (Issues 4 and 5).**
   - Dan Rourke has said we will circulate an execution version of the Seller Note.
   - The "Company Products" definition and the Delaware governing-law and forum clause must be fixed before Peitort signs.

Issues 1 (uncapped guarantee indemnity) and 3 (tax survival gap) are in the signed SPA. Fixing them requires a written amendment signed by both Parties under SPA Section 11.8. The best time to get that amendment is now, while Seller still wants things from us (the side letter and a smooth Closing).

**Key background terms**

| Term | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Base Purchase Price | $186,000,000, paid as $162,000,000 cash plus a $24,000,000 Seller Note | SPA §§2.1, 2.2(b) |
| Seller Note | Matures 36 months after Closing; 6% simple interest | Note §§2.1, 3.1 |
| General Cap | 10% of the Base Purchase Price ($18,600,000) | SPA §9.6(a) |
| General survival period | 12 months | SPA §9.1 |
| Governing law and forum | New York law; New York County courts | SPA §§11.10, 11.11 |
| Order of precedence | The SPA prevails over the Ancillary Agreements, **except that the Seller Note governs its own payment, set-off and dispute resolution terms** | SPA §11.6 |

Several issues below turn on the Section 11.6 exception.

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Uncapped Buyer indemnity for Seller Guarantees, including pre-Closing defaults

**Location:** SPA Section 9.3(c), read with Sections 9.6(b) and 9.4. Related definitions are "Seller Guarantees" in Section 1.1 and Schedules 4.8 (item 5.1), 4.9 (items 6.2(a) and 6.4) and 4.19 (item 13.2).

**What it says**
- Section 9.3(c) requires Buyer to indemnify the Seller Indemnified Parties for all Losses from any payment or performance under any Seller Guarantee, "whether arising before or after the Closing."
- The Seller Guarantees cover two contracts:
  - the Bridgewater Facility Lease, which runs to March 31, 2033 and has two five-year renewal options; and
  - the Kessington API Supply Agreement, which runs to August 31, 2029.
- Section 9.6(b) caps Buyer's liability only for claims under Section 9.3(a).
- Nothing in Section 9.6 refers to Section 9.3(c).
- The Deductible in Section 9.4 applies only to claims under Section 9.2(a).

**Why it matters**
- Peitort's exposure under Section 9.3(c) has no dollar limit and no basket.
- The exposure could last more than 16 years if the lease renewals are exercised.
- The words "before or after the Closing" make Peitort reimburse Seller even for defaults by the Company while Seller owned and controlled it, such as unpaid pre-Closing rent or API purchase shortfalls. Seller should bear those losses.
- The result reverses the normal allocation of risk. Peitort would be paying for losses caused by Seller's own mismanagement.
- Separately, Section 9.3(b) (Buyer's breach of covenant, including covenants under the Seller Note) is also outside the cap. That is more customary, but we should keep it in mind.

**Recommended fix**, in order of preference:
1. Amend the SPA to require that the Seller Guarantees be released, or replaced with Peitort guarantees, at Closing. Make the release a Seller deliverable under Section 3.2, so that Section 9.3(c) falls away.
2. If a release cannot be obtained in time:
   - delete "whether arising before or after the Closing" and limit Section 9.3(c) to obligations that first arise and relate to periods after Closing;
   - add an express Seller indemnity under Section 9.2 for pre-Closing defaults under the guaranteed contracts; and
   - extend Section 9.6(b) to cover Section 9.3(c) with an agreed cap and a sunset date.
3. Add a covenant requiring both Parties to keep using efforts to obtain the releases after Closing.

---

### Issue 2: The side letter strips the regulatory-compliance carve-out from the General Cap (URGENT)

**Location:** Seller side letter draft, Section 2 (Sections 2.1–2.3). It conflicts with SPA Section 9.6(c) and LOI Section 5(d).

**What it says**
- Section 2.1 is framed as an amendment under SPA Section 11.8.
- Section 2.2 amends SPA Section 9.6(c) "by deleting the words 'or Section 4.12 (Regulatory Compliance)'."
- Section 2.3 provides that the letter "shall form part of the Agreement."
- The rest of the letter is benign and buries the change:
  - Section 3 deals with termination of the Management Services Agreement.
  - Section 4 covers wire-fraud protocols and settling the forms of closing certificates.

**Why it matters**
- Currently, Losses from a breach of Section 4.12 (FDA, cGMP and permits) are capped only at the Purchase Price.
- If Peitort signs, those Losses fall under the **$18,600,000 General Cap**. That is roughly 10% of the price, for the highest-risk area of a sterile-injectable manufacturer.
- The risk is concrete. Schedule 4.12 discloses:
  - a 2023 FDA Form 483 at the Bridgewater facility; and
  - the 2024–25 market withdrawal of Lorvexa.
- The regulatory carve-out was an agreed deal term in LOI Section 5(d). Seller is trying to reopen it through a closing letter.
- The precedence clause does not protect us. Section 2.3 makes the letter part of the SPA itself, not an "Ancillary Agreement," so Section 11.6 has nothing to resolve. Once signed, the letter is a valid Section 11.8 amendment.
- **Authority point:** the board consent authorizes the officers to make only changes "not materially adverse to the Corporation." Removing this carve-out is arguably materially adverse. An officer who signs it may be acting outside the board's authorization.

**Recommended fix**
- Advise the client not to sign the side letter as drafted.
- Send back a revised letter with Section 2 deleted entirely, and Section 5.1 conformed. Sections 3 and 4 are acceptable and can stay.
- If Seller insists on reopening the cap, treat that as a negotiation that requires board approval and real consideration. One option is a trade for the fixes in Issues 1, 3 and 6.

---

### Issue 3: The tax indemnity expires 12 months after Closing

**Location:** SPA Section 9.2(c), read with Section 9.1 and the definition of "Fundamental Representations" in Section 1.1.

**What it says**
- Section 9.2(c) is the pre-Closing tax indemnity. Claims under it "may be made only during the survival period applicable to the representations and warranties in Section 4.11."
- Under Section 9.1, representations survive 12 months, except Fundamental Representations, which survive six years.
- Fundamental Representations are defined as Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 and 4.20. The tax representation (Section 4.11) is not included.
- The indemnity therefore ends **12 months after Closing**.

**Why it matters**
- The IRS generally has three years after a return is filed to assess tax (IRC §6501), and longer in some cases. State limitations periods are similar or longer.
- Most pre-Closing tax exposure (2023–2026 returns) will be assessable long after the indemnity has expired.
- Under Section 6.6(a), Seller prepares the Company's pre-Closing returns that are due after Closing. Some of those returns may not be audited, or even filed, until late in the 12-month window.
- New York law (SPA Section 11.10) generally enforces contractual survival periods that shorten the statutory limitations period. The 12-month limit will likely be upheld.
- Peitort would then bear Seller's pre-Closing taxes, contrary to LOI Section 5(e).

**Recommended fix**
- Amend Sections 9.1 and 9.2(c) so that the tax representations in Section 4.11 and the Section 9.2(c) indemnity survive until 60 days after the applicable statute of limitations expires, including extensions and waivers.
- Confirm that the Section 9.2(c) indemnity is not subject to the Deductible or the General Cap. As drafted it is not, because those limits apply only to Section 9.2(a), but we should state this expressly for clarity.

---

### Issue 4: The Seller Note's narrower "Company Products" definition blocks set-off for Lorvexa losses (URGENT: before Note execution)

**Location:**
- Seller Note Section 1.1 ("Company Products" means "the products listed on Exhibit A") and Section 4.1.
- Compare SPA Section 1.1 ("Company Products" means all products manufactured, sold or distributed "at any time prior to the Closing") and SPA Sections 9.2(d), 9.9 and 11.6.

**What it says**
- Under SPA Section 9.2(d), Seller indemnifies Buyer for Product Liability Claims relating to Company Products, using the broad SPA definition. That covers the pending Lorvexa cases on Schedule 4.15:
  - *Dunmore* (D.N.J.);
  - *Pereira* (Phila. C.C.P.);
  - *Holcombe* (Fla. Cir. Ct.); and
  - the August 12, 2026 demand letter.
- SPA Section 9.9 makes Buyer's set-off right "subject to the terms of the Seller Note."
- Under SPA Section 11.6, the Seller Note governs set-off.
- Seller Note Section 4.1 allows set-off only for Product Liability Claims relating to "Company Products" as the Note defines them.
- Exhibit A to the Note lists only Velnarix and Ostrevan. **Lorvexa is not listed.**

**Why it matters**
- The Lorvexa claims are the most significant known product-liability exposure. The insurer has accepted coverage only under a reservation of rights.
- Peitort will have a contractual indemnity for those claims but **cannot set off Lorvexa Losses against the $24,000,000 Seller Note**. It must keep paying principal and interest and sue Seller separately.
- The Seller Note is the main security for Seller's indemnity obligations, so this gap defeats much of the Note's purpose.
- There is a related default risk. Note Section 7.1(a) excuses only amounts "withheld or set off under Section 4." If Peitort withholds for a Lorvexa Loss, the withholding falls outside Section 4. That could be an Event of Default, triggering default interest under Section 3.4 and acceleration under Section 7.2.
- **Broader point:** Note Section 4.1 allows set-off only for product-liability Losses. It does not cover tax, regulatory, general representation or covenant claims. That is narrower than SPA Section 9.9 ("any amount to which any Buyer Indemnified Party is entitled under this Article IX"). It is also narrower than LOI Section 3(f), which contemplated set-off "for amounts owed to Buyer under the indemnification provisions."

**Recommended fix**
- Before signing the execution version, conform Note Section 1.1 to the SPA definition. Either delete the Note's own definition and rely on the SPA term through Note Section 1.2, or expressly include Lorvexa and every product sold before Closing.
- Expand Note Section 4.1 to allow set-off for any amount owed to a Buyer Indemnified Party under SPA Article IX.
- SPA Section 2.2(b) requires the Note to be only "substantially in the form" of Exhibit B. Conforming the Note to the SPA's own definition and to the LOI's set-off term is a defensible request.

---

### Issue 5: Delaware law and forum in the Seller Note split set-off disputes from the New York indemnity claims (URGENT: before Note execution)

**Location:** Seller Note Section 10.1 ("laws of the State of Delaware") and Section 10.2 ("exclusive jurisdiction of the Superior Court of the State of Delaware"). Compare SPA Sections 11.10 (New York law), 11.11 (exclusive jurisdiction of the New York County courts, "including any claim for indemnification under Article IX") and 11.6.

**What it says**
- Because SPA Section 11.6 gives the Seller Note control over "payment, set-off and dispute resolution," the Note's Delaware clause will govern any dispute over whether Peitort may withhold or set off.
- Note Section 4.3 confirms this. Disputed set-offs are resolved by a final judgment "under Section 10," which means in Delaware.
- The underlying question of whether Seller owes the indemnity must be litigated in New York County under New York law.

**Why it matters**
- **The Seller Note is governed by Delaware law, not New York law.**
- Peitort faces parallel proceedings on the same Losses in two courts under two bodies of law. That raises costs and the risk of inconsistent results.
- Seller could sue on the Note in Delaware for non-payment while the indemnity claim is still pending in New York. Peitort would face acceleration and collection costs (Note Sections 7.2 and 7.3) before the New York court rules.
- The two contract-law regimes may diverge, for example on the enforceability of survival limits and on how set-off rights are treated.

**Recommended fix**
- Amend the execution version of Note Section 10 to adopt New York law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the state or federal courts in New York County, matching SPA Sections 11.10 and 11.11.
- At a minimum, provide that any dispute over the entitlement underlying a set-off is resolved solely in the SPA forum, and that the Note court is bound by that determination.
- Make the same corresponding change in Note Section 4.3.

---

### Issue 6: The Orlund change-of-control consent is not a closing condition, and Peitort has no remedy (MOST URGENT)

**Location:**
- Disclosure Schedule 4.4, item 2.1.
- SPA Sections 7.2(d), 6.4, 6.8 and 9.2(a), and the definition of "Required Consents" in Section 1.1.
- Schedule 7.2(d), which lists only the four state board of pharmacy approvals.

**What it says**
- Section 14.3 of the Exclusive License Agreement requires Orlund's prior written consent to any change of control of the Company. Orlund may terminate the license if consent is not obtained.
- Schedule 4.4 confirms that this transaction is a change of control. The only step disclosed is a notice to Orlund dated August 27, 2026. Nothing shows that consent has been requested in proper form or granted.
- "Required Consents" are only the items on Schedule 7.2(d), all of which are state boards of pharmacy. The Orlund consent is not among them.

**Why it matters**
- **The Orlund consent is not a condition to Peitort's obligation to close.** Section 7.2(d) covers only Required Consents.
- Seller has no covenant to obtain it. The reasonable-best-efforts covenant in Section 6.4 covers only Required Consents.
- Section 6.8 requires notice only of facts affecting the Section 7.2 conditions.
- Because the consent requirement is disclosed against Section 4.4, its absence is not a breach of representation. It cannot support a claim under Section 9.2(a), and it does not cause a failure of the bring-down condition in Section 7.2(a).
- The MAE condition in Section 7.2(f) does not protect against a termination by Orlund after Closing.
- Peitort could pay $186,000,000 and then lose the license to Velnarix, the Company's lead product, which is protected by licensed patents running to 2034 and 2036. Peitort would have no recourse against Seller.
- The closing email thread (November 17) describes California as "the only Required Consent outstanding." That confirms neither side is tracking Orlund.
- MCA Section 6.1 bars Peitort from contacting the Company's licensors about the deal without Bratousk's written consent. Peitort cannot easily approach Orlund directly.

**Recommended fix** (needs a Seller-signed SPA amendment under Section 11.8 before the week of December 7):
1. Add the Orlund consent, in a form reasonably satisfactory to Buyer, to Schedule 7.2(d) as a Required Consent. This brings it within both the Section 7.2(d) closing condition and Seller's Section 6.4 covenant.
2. As a fallback or supplement, obtain a specific Seller indemnity under Section 9.2 for all Losses from any termination or adverse modification of the Exclusive License Agreement arising from the change of control. Make that indemnity uncapped by the General Cap and subject to set-off under the Seller Note (see Issue 4). An escrow or holdback would add further protection.
3. Immediately ask Seller for:
   - the status of the Orlund request; and
   - written consent under MCA Section 6.1 for Peitort to join discussions with Orlund.
4. If Seller refuses, the Section 8.1(b) outside date of January 31, 2027 gives some time, but Peitort should not close without the protections above. Seller's request for the side letter gives us practical leverage.

---

## III. Other Observations (non-urgent)

- **Seller Note §6.2 drafting error.** Section 6.2 refers to a payment block "under clause (ii) above," but the section has no clause (ii). Clean this up in the execution version so the 179-day block limit is enforceable.
- **Board consent.** The consent approves the SPA and the Note "substantially in the form presented" and authorizes changes only if they are not materially adverse. The side letter amendment (Issue 2) would likely need fresh board approval. The proposed fixes to Issues 1 and 3–6 favor Peitort and are within the officers' authority.
- **Key Employee Agreement.** No material issues. It is governed by New Jersey law, which is appropriate for the Bridgewater employee. Section 7.2(e) of the SPA preserves Peitort's walk right if Dr. Sallow repudiates.
- **LOI, email thread and MCA.** No independent issues. The LOI supports our positions on Issues 2, 3 and 4. The email thread confirms Issue 6, and its wire-verification protocol is sound. The MCA restriction on contact with the licensor is relevant to Issue 6.

---

## IV. Recommended Next Steps

| Priority | Action | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Raise the Orlund consent with Seller's counsel (Celia Marchetti); propose an SPA amendment adding it to Schedule 7.2(d) plus a specific indemnity; request MCA §6.1 consent to contact Orlund | This week |
| 2 | Return the side letter with Section 2 deleted; advise the client not to sign the current draft | This week |
| 3 | Revise the Seller Note execution version: SPA definition of "Company Products," set-off for all Article IX claims, New York law and forum, fix §6.2 | Before the execution version circulates |
| 4 | Propose an SPA amendment for Issues 1 and 3 (release of guarantees or capped post-Closing indemnity; tax survival to the statute of limitations plus 60 days), packaged with item 1 | Before Closing |
| 5 | Brief the client's General Counsel and, if Seller pushes the cap change, the board | Before Closing |

Please let me know if you would like me to prepare the amendment and markups.

|---|---|---|---|

- SPA § 11.6 (Order of Precedence) says the SPA prevails over Ancillary Agreements, *"except that the Seller Note shall govern with respect to its payment, set-off and dispute resolution terms."*
- SPA § 9.9 makes Buyer's set-off right "subject to the terms of the Seller Note."

Because the Note has not yet been executed, the execution-version circulation described in Dan Rourke's November 9 email is our point of leverage.

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Orlund change-of-control consent is neither a closing condition nor indemnifiable (URGENT)

**Where it appears**
- Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 4.4, item 2.1.
- SPA § 1.1 (definition of "Required Consents").
- SPA § 6.4 (Required Consents covenant).
- SPA § 7.2(d) (closing condition).
- SPA Schedule 7.2(d).

**What the documents say**
- Schedule 4.4 discloses that § 14.3 of the Orlund Exclusive License Agreement requires Orlund's *prior written consent* to any change of control of the Company. The sale of more than 50% of the voting securities counts as a change of control.
- Orlund may terminate the license if a change of control occurs without its consent.
- The Company only *gave notice* to Orlund, on August 27, 2026. Nothing in the file shows that Orlund has consented.

**Why the protections do not reach it**
- **Closing condition.** SPA § 7.2(d) conditions Buyer's obligation to close on "each Required Consent shall have been obtained." Required Consents are defined as the items on Schedule 7.2(d). That schedule lists only the four state board of pharmacy approvals (NJ, CA, TX, FL). The Orlund consent is not on it.
- **Seller covenant.** Seller's efforts covenant in § 6.4 extends only to Required Consents.
- **Indemnity.** The consent requirement is disclosed against the § 4.4 representation. Its absence therefore is not a breach that Peitort could claim under § 9.2(a).

**Why it matters**
- The obligation to close is triggered only by the state pharmacy approvals. Three of them are in, and California is expected by month-end. Once California arrives, Peitort could be obliged to close (absent a separate MAE argument) even though Orlund has not consented.
- Orlund could then terminate the license for Velnarix, the Company's lead product and the core of the deal's value.
- Peitort would have no closing-condition walk right and no indemnity claim. The closing-logistics thread treats California as the only outstanding gating item. The Orlund consent does not appear on anyone's checklist.

**Recommended fix**
- **Primary fix.** Before California approval issues, negotiate an amendment under SPA § 11.8 that:
  - adds the Orlund written consent (in form reasonably satisfactory to Buyer, including a waiver of the § 14.3 termination right) to Schedule 7.2(d) as a Required Consent; and
  - by doing so, brings the consent within both the § 7.2(d) condition and the § 6.4 reasonable-best-efforts covenant.
- **Fallback.** Obtain a specific, uncapped (or Purchase-Price-capped) Seller indemnity for all Losses arising from any Orlund termination or renegotiation tied to the change of control. That indemnity should be expressly set-off-eligible under the Seller Note.
- **Immediate steps.**
  - Ask Bratousk's counsel today for the status of the Orlund request.
  - Add the Orlund consent to the closing checklist.
  - Do not agree a Closing Date until this is resolved.
- **Contact restriction.** Note that § 6.1 of the Mutual Confidentiality Agreement bars Peitort from contacting Orlund without Bratousk's consent. Any direct outreach should be cleared with Bratousk first.

---

### Issue 2: The draft side letter removes the regulatory-compliance carve-out from the General Cap (URGENT: do not sign)

**Where it appears:** Seller Side Letter (draft), Section 2 (§§ 2.1–2.3).

**What the side letter does**
- SPA § 9.6(c) excludes three categories from the $18,600,000 General Cap:
  - Fraud;
  - breaches of Fundamental Representations; and
  - breaches of **Section 4.12 (Regulatory Compliance)**.
- That carve-out tracks § 5(d) of the June 2026 LOI, which expressly listed the regulatory compliance representation as an agreed carve-out.
- Side letter § 2.2 deletes the words "or Section 4.12 (Regulatory Compliance)" from § 9.6(c).
- Side letter § 2.1 invokes SPA § 11.8 as an amendment signed by each Party.
- Side letter § 2.3 provides that the letter "shall form part of the Agreement."

**Why it matters**
- Because the side letter becomes part of the SPA rather than an Ancillary Agreement, the § 11.6 precedence clause would not protect Peitort.
- If Peitort signs, Seller's liability for breaches of § 4.12 would be capped at the General Cap of $18,600,000 instead of the Purchase Price. That representation covers FDCA and cGMP compliance, permits and FDA correspondence.
- This is a significant economic concession. The Company is a sterile-injectable manufacturer. It has a 2023 Form 483 and a 2024–25 market withdrawal of Lorvexa (Schedule 4.12). Regulatory exposure is among the most material risks in the deal.
- Regulatory claims would also compete for the same $18.6 million with all other general rep claims.
- The amendment is buried in a letter whose other sections are routine:
  - Section 3 covers termination of the Management Services Agreement.
  - Section 4 covers wire-fraud and certificate mechanics.

**Recommended fix**
- Do not sign Section 2. Respond with a revised side letter that deletes Section 2 entirely and retains only Sections 3–6.
- Conform § 5.1 ("Except as amended by Section 2…").
- Remind Bratousk that the carve-out was agreed at the LOI stage.
- Confirm with Peitort Legal that no one on the business side has signed or is about to sign the draft.
- If Bratousk insists on some limit, the most Peitort should consider is a separate, higher regulatory cap (for example, 50% of the Purchase Price). Any such concession requires client sign-off.

---

### Issue 3: Uncapped Buyer indemnity for the Seller Guarantees, including pre-Closing obligations

**Where it appears:** SPA § 9.3(c), read with §§ 9.6(b) and 9.4; definition of "Seller Guarantees" in § 1.1.

**What the SPA says**
- Under § 9.3(c), Peitort must indemnify the Seller Indemnified Parties for "any payment or performance by any Seller Indemnified Party under any Seller Guarantee, *whether arising before or after the Closing*."
- The Seller Guarantees are Bratousk's guaranties of:
  - the Facility Lease, the Bridgewater lease running through March 31, 2033 with two five-year renewal options; and
  - the API Supply Agreement with Kessington, running through August 31, 2029 (Schedules 4.8, 4.9 item 6.4).

**Why it matters**
- **No cap.** Section 9.6(b) caps Buyer's liability only for claims under § 9.3(a). Nothing in § 9.6 refers to § 9.3(c). The Deductible in § 9.4 applies only to § 9.2(a). The guarantee indemnity therefore has no cap and no deductible.
- **Pre-Closing exposure shifts to Buyer.** The words "whether arising before or after the Closing" make Peitort reimburse Bratousk even for guarantee calls triggered by the Company's *pre-Closing* defaults under the lease or supply agreement. Those are periods when Bratousk owned and controlled the Company. This shifts to Peitort exposure that should sit with the Seller. It may also overlap with matters for which Seller owes Peitort indemnity, creating circular claims.
- **Long tail.** The lease runs for roughly another 6.5 years, plus possible renewals. The resulting exposure is open-ended in both amount and duration.

**Recommended fix**
- **Preferred.** Require Bratousk to obtain releases of both guaranties at Closing, with Peitort or the Company providing replacement credit support. Make the releases a Seller closing deliverable under § 3.2 and delete § 9.3(c).
- **Fallback.** Revise § 9.3(c) so that it:
  - is limited to obligations "arising after the Closing";
  - excludes any Losses attributable to pre-Closing breaches by the Company or matters for which Seller owes indemnity under § 9.2;
  - adds § 9.3(c) to the § 9.6(b) cap (or a separate dollar cap); and
  - requires Buyer to use commercially reasonable efforts to procure releases after Closing, with the indemnity ending on release.

---

### Issue 4: Seller Note's narrow "Company Products" definition blocks set-off for Lorvexa product liability Losses (URGENT: before Note execution)

**Where it appears**
- Seller Note § 1 (definition of "Company Products").
- Seller Note § 4.1 (Right of Set-Off).
- Seller Note Exhibit A.
- Compare SPA § 1.1 ("Company Products") and § 9.9 (Right of Set-Off).

**The two definitions**
- **SPA definition.** "Company Products" means all products manufactured, sold or distributed by the Company "*at any time prior to the Closing*." This definition drives the specific product liability indemnity in § 9.2(d), which expressly covers the pending claims on Schedule 4.15. Those claims are:
  - three suits relating to the discontinued **Lorvexa** oral suspension (*Dunmore*, *Pereira*, *Holcombe*); and
  - an August 2026 demand letter from two further claimants.
- **Seller Note definition.** Seller Note § 4.1 permits set-off only for Losses from Product Liability Claims "relating to Company Products." The Note's § 1 defines that term as "the products listed on Exhibit A." Exhibit A lists only **Velnarix and Ostrevan**. Lorvexa is not on it.

**Why it matters**
- SPA § 9.9 makes set-off "subject to the terms of the Seller Note," and § 11.6 gives the Note control over its set-off terms. The narrower Note definition therefore prevails for set-off purposes.
- Peitort would be indemnified for Lorvexa Losses under the SPA, but could not withhold them from the $24,000,000 Note. It would have to pay the Note in full and pursue Bratousk separately for recovery.
- Lorvexa is the *only* known product liability exposure. The insurer has accepted coverage under a reservation of rights, and the product liability policy carries a $250,000 retention. The set-off right was the main practical security for that indemnity.
- Separately, § 4.1 limits set-off to product liability Losses only. This is narrower than LOI § 3(f), which contemplated set-off for amounts owed under "the indemnification provisions of the Definitive Agreement" generally.

**Recommended fix**
- In the execution version of the Note, delete the Exhibit A definition. Replace it with: "Company Products" has the meaning given in the Purchase Agreement.
- Delete Exhibit A.
- Broaden § 4.1 so set-off extends to *any* amount to which a Buyer Indemnified Party is entitled under Article IX of the SPA, consistent with the LOI and with SPA § 9.9.
- Fix this before the execution version is circulated. Our own November 9 email commits us to circulating the Note "in the form of Exhibit B."

### Issue 5: Seller Note's Delaware governing law and forum control set-off disputes, splitting them from New York indemnity claims

**Where it appears**
- Seller Note § 10.1 (Delaware law) and § 10.2 (exclusive jurisdiction of the Superior Court of the State of Delaware).
- Compare SPA § 11.10 (New York law), § 11.11 (exclusive jurisdiction of state or federal courts in New York County, expressly including indemnification claims under Article IX) and § 11.6 (Order of Precedence).

**The conflict**
- Seller Note § 10.1 expressly applies Delaware law to "any dispute regarding payment or set-off under it."
- Because SPA § 11.6 lets the Seller Note govern its own payment, set-off *and dispute resolution* terms, the Delaware clause controls.

**Why it matters**
- If Peitort withholds a Note payment for an indemnified Loss and Bratousk disputes it, two proceedings can result:
  - the dispute over the withholding goes to the Delaware Superior Court under Delaware law; and
  - the underlying indemnity claim (whether Seller in fact owes the Loss) must go to New York County under New York law.
- Peitort faces parallel proceedings, duplicated cost, and the risk of inconsistent outcomes on the same Losses.
- The specific danger is a Delaware court finding the set-off improper before the New York court has ruled on the indemnity. That could let Bratousk call an Event of Default and **accelerate** the Note under § 7.2, with default interest under § 3.4 and collection costs under § 7.3.
- Note § 4.3 ties final resolution of a disputed set-off to a "final, non-appealable judgment under Section 10." That means a Delaware judgment, which compounds the problem.

**Recommended fix**
- Conform Seller Note § 10 to the SPA:
  - New York governing law (matching § 11.10); and
  - exclusive jurisdiction of the state or federal courts in New York County (matching § 11.11).
- Add language that any set-off dispute shall be resolved together with the related indemnification claim under the SPA.
- Revise SPA § 11.6 so the Note's "dispute resolution terms" no longer prevail over the SPA. At a minimum, provide that the SPA governs any dispute over entitlement to indemnification underlying a set-off.
- Make these changes in the same execution version as the Issue 4 fixes.
